Moment 3: When a Team Has a Breakthrough Worth Scaling

One of Ember's regional sales teams built an AI process that automates pipeline generation. In six months, the team cut prospecting time by half and now spends that time closing deals.

The COO wants it live in every market by early next year. The other regional sales heads aren't convinced. Three objections keep coming up:

"Our sales cycles are longer and relationship-driven."
"Our data isn't clean enough for this."
"We'd have to drop tools we've already invested in."

The COO has asked for your recommendation, not just a reaction.

What do you recommend? Brainstorm at your table.

AI Simulation

Dallas, Houston, Chicago, San Francisco

The financial services industry is being squeezed from both ends. Clients want faster loan decisions and lower fees in the same breath, while AI-powered underwriting and robo-advisory tools are collapsing the advantage that used to come from an experienced relationship manager's judgment. AI-native fintech entrants are going after the core lending and wealth management business traditional institutions built their reputation on. The same clients asking for a better rate are also asking for AI-enabled portfolio reporting, faster underwriting decisions, and risk analytics that used to take weeks to produce. For a firm whose entire value proposition is speed and accuracy in putting capital to work for clients, standing still is not an option.

Indigo has felt that pressure directly. Built over decades into one of the industry's major financial institutions, Indigo operates through specialized business units — lending and underwriting, wealth management, risk and compliance, finance, HR, and IT — each with its own systems, leadership, and definition of success, serving clients across dozens of regional markets. That structure is Indigo's strength: deep expertise in each function, close proximity to the regional markets it serves, an entrepreneurial culture inside every unit. Lately, it has also become its biggest liability.

Over the past year, nearly every business unit and shared-service function — lending, wealth management, risk and compliance, finance, HR, and IT — has started building its own AI solution: smarter underwriting models, automated fraud detection, AI-assisted portfolio recommendations. The energy is real. So is the mess. Several use cases are now in flight across the enterprise with no shared way to compare them, let alone fund them together. Pilots are running at different speeds against different definitions of success.

The real question Indigo is facing isn't whether AI can underwrite loans faster or flag fraud quicker. It's whether its leaders can move at the pace AI now demands — and do it well, in a way that elevates human potential rather than leaves it behind. That's the leader this moment is asking you to be.

A: Tell the working group: "Before we score anything, let's agree how we'll decide." Build criteria together, then score all twelve the same way, your own three included. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "If your case is strong, criteria we all trust will show it."

B: Meet every sponsor, including the one who stayed behind. Ask what each case needs and relies on, then share the patterns with the group before you recommend. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "Help me understand what success looks like for you."

C: Take a view to the CTO: "I think this portfolio has to prove one thing: cost, growth or capability. Which, and is three the right number?" Pause the working group until you agree. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "I want to solve the right problem before I decide where yours fits."

D: Propose to the CTO: two-week trials on five or six cases, with the results choosing the top three before the deadline. Tell the lobbying sponsor: "Let's test it. A strong result is the best argument you can bring."

The CTO has asked you to bring the executive team a recommended portfolio of three funded AI initiatives in four weeks. Your working group has surfaced twelve use cases from across Ember's business units and functions. Each has a sponsor, and several already have polished decks.

No one has agreed how to decide. Every sponsor believes their case belongs in the top three. Two cases share an executive sponsor who expects both to go forward. After the last session, one sponsor stayed behind: "I've been told this is the highest-value initiative in the portfolio. If it's not in the top three, I need to understand why."

You have a strong view on which three are the real bets. You also know the executive team wants momentum, not another process.

What do you do?

The criteria session is uncomfortable but productive. Sponsors realize they've been defining "value" differently, and the agreed scorecard earns real buy-in. The cost is two of your four weeks, and the criteria miss one case that doesn't fit any category. The shared definition holds, but the executive team asks why speed to value wasn't weighted higher.

Your sponsor conversations reveal that four cases depend on the same data foundation, and two overlap almost entirely. You merge them and your recommendation lands with the group. But sponsors were candid with you and guarded with each other, and a week of meetings leaves less time than you wanted to test the shortlist.

The CTO pushes back on "three initiatives." The real aim is to show the board a credible AI return before year-end, which changes which cases rank. Your reframe saves weeks of debate. But the working group sat idle while you escalated, and several sponsors feel the process moved above their heads.

The trials surface a surprise. The most polished deck stalls on data quality and a modest case delivers results in ten days. The executive team backs the top three on evidence. But two weeks of trials stretched the team thin, and the cases that never got a trial slot feel overlooked.

A: Tell the truth: "Yes. There have been leadership conversations about whether to continue the pilot. Nothing is decided, but I want you to know. I've been shielding you and the team from those discussions so you could focus on the work. Given where we are, let's reset milestones together and define what a meaningful win looks like in the next 60 days."

B: Say: "I hear you. I think the team needs a fresh perspective. Let me bring in an AI implementation expert who has helped other teams through similar challenges. They'll join your next meeting, share what's worked elsewhere, and help the team think through where to focus."

C: Say: "The honest answer is that this pilot has run into challenges more runway won't fix. I want to recommend we document what we've learned, protect the team's reputation, and redirect resources to a higher-confidence initiative. This isn't failure, it's how Ember learns. I want to make sure you and the team are well positioned for what comes next."
Moment 2: When AI innovation creates uncertainty

The CFO has named a reporting automation pilot as one of Ember's highest-priority AI initiatives: cut manual reporting time by 35% and improve first-pass accuracy. Your direct report leads the pilot team, eight people who took it on with genuine enthusiasm.

Manual reporting time is down 14%: real progress, but short of the 35% target. The team is running at an unsustainable pace. The CFO has asked for weekly progress reports for six weeks, which the team experiences as surveillance. You've been absorbing the pressure. When your direct report has asked how the CFO feels, you've said the CFO appreciates the effort, which is true but incomplete.

What you haven't shared: the senior leadership team has discussed whether to continue the pilot or redirect resources. Two of the team's strongest contributors are quietly weighing opportunities elsewhere in the company.

Your direct report comes to you: "The team is exhausted. I'm getting the sense the CFO isn't just asking for updates to celebrate us. Is there something I should know?"

What do you do?
Moment 2: When AI innovation creates uncertainty

Your direct report is relieved. The news isn't good, but the uncertainty is gone. You share the context with the team, own the gap between what you said and what you knew, and set two reset milestones. The two contributors considering leaving stay. One later says: "I didn't need it to be easy. I needed to know you were telling us what was real."

The expert is skilled, but their arrival tells the team that leadership doubts them. Your direct report asked a direct question and got outside help instead. The two contributors make their decisions, and trust in you drops. The real problem, a depleted team working without full context, goes untouched.

The framing lands, and the CFO agrees to redirect. The two contributors stay. The pilot closes with a knowledge-capture session. It can be the right call, but works best after an honest look at whether a reset could have worked. Your direct report later wonders if it could have.

NEW INFORMATION

Eight weeks have passed since you spoke directly with Jordan and the team. The numbers back up what you hoped: the pulse survey shows trust in leadership has rebounded, and Jordan says the team feels informed and respected again. Expenditure, the global consulting firm already assessing delivery progress elsewhere in the transformation, was also commissioned to run a culture pulse across every pilot population.

On paper, your fix worked.

But their report surfaces something you didn't see coming. Two people on pilot teams adjacent to Jordan's (teams that had been watching this situation from the outside) resigned this month. Their exit interviews cite "no confidence that leadership will tell us the truth before it's decided for us." Meanwhile, Jordan's team has quietly been asked to help onboard two other pilot teams onto the financial administration workflow, on top of their own target. Jordan hasn't complained. Neither has anyone else.

Force rank the factors you think are most responsible for this emerging risk, from greatest to least.

Jordan's team needed direct reassurance from you, but that moment needed to become a repeatable standard for communicating struggling pilots enterprise-wide, not a one-off fix.
You addressed what your team needed to hear, but not what the organization needed to see, leaving other teams to fill the silence with their own worst assumptions.
Trust was rebuilt with Jordan's team, but the honesty you modeled never reached the teams watching from outside — where that same uncertainty is now resurfacing.
Morale recovered because the immediate threat was removed, but the underlying capacity problem was never solved — one team is still doing the work of three.

D is most responsible. The real gap isn't anything you did with Jordan's team — it's that you treated a hard moment as a one-time interpersonal fix instead of turning it into how the organization handles any struggling pilot. That gap explains both symptoms at once: the trust problem in teams you never personally reassured, and the fact that nobody has a mechanism to flag Jordan's team quietly taking on more work. It's the systemic root, not just a local miss.

A and C are next, roughly tied. Both correctly diagnose the trust half of the problem — the honesty that worked inside Jordan's team never traveled outward. A frames it as a relationship-equity gap, C frames it as an organizational-visibility gap. They're really the same insight from two angles, and either is a defensible second place. Between the two, I'd put A very slightly ahead, since "relationship equity" is the more precise mechanism — it explains why the same message wouldn't have landed the same way with teams who don't have that history with you, where C's framing is a bit more generic.

B is least responsible, by design. It's true, and it's a real problem, but it was never the thing this moment asked you to solve — you were managing a trust and communication crisis, not a staffing-capacity one. Using it to explain the resignations is a reach: adjacent teams didn't quit because Jordan's team is overloaded, they quit because they don't trust leadership to tell them the truth. B is a correct observation about a different, parallel issue, which makes it the weakest answer to "what's responsible for this risk."

A: You recommend a fast rollout, telling Mia "The business case is proven, and every week we wait, eight teams run the old process. Let's get them started, they can document as they go. I'm available for questions if you or the team have any."

B: You set a six-week pilot timeline with a clear documentation plan, telling Mia: "You're right to flag this, so let's just run parallel pilots with two volunteer teams first. Document what's working as you teach it, built into the pilot itself. We'll co-build the enterprise template with you, not around you, then we scale."

C: You recommend coordinating a multi-team review process, telling Mia: "Before we roll anything out, let's do this properly. We'll pause and stand up a documentation workstream first. I'll loop in operations, compliance, and the receiving teams so we build the standard with full input. Once everyone signs off, we scale."
Moment 4: When a Team Has a Breakthrough Worth Scaling

Mia leads Candidate Screening and her team built an AI workflow that cut processing time by 40% and improved first-pass accuracy. Leadership noticed the improvement, yet they're not aware that the workflow was never formally documented. It relies on Mia's institutional knowledge, two analysts who know which candidates the model misreads, and calibration decisions never written down.

The team is at capacity, and there is pressure to replicate the workflow across eight teams by end of quarter. Mia comes to you: "I'm being pressured to roll this out by end of quarter. I want to make it work, but I'm worried. We built it iteratively, a lot isn't written down, and some of it only makes sense if you've been in the weeds. I don't want to hand people a black box." What you decide will shape not just this rollout, but how Meridian treats every future breakthrough from a team that moved fast.

What do you do?
Moment 4: When a Team Has a Breakthrough Worth Scaling

Six of the eight teams adopt the workflow. Turnaround improves in three. The other three hit edge cases the documentation doesn't cover and get inconsistent results. Within two months, four different versions run across the function. No one can say with confidence which is performing best or why. Fast deployment without documentation fragments the knowledge that made the breakthrough possible. The teams that built it get blamed for a rollout failure that was actually a documentation failure.

There is pushback on the timeline, but you hold the position: scaling without documentation fragments the knowledge that made the breakthrough possible and produces inconsistent results across teams. Two pilot teams are selected. Mia co-facilitates the onboarding, and documentation is built in real time as edge cases surface. Six weeks later, the enterprise template is solid and the rollout to the remaining six teams goes cleanly. It takes longer up front, but the result is replicable, measurable, and compounds over time.

The documentation workstream kicks off. Stakeholder alignment takes longer than expected: each group has questions and requests for review. Mia and her analysts are pulled into meeting after meeting. Six weeks pass with no rollout started. By the time sign-off arrives, two target teams have built their own workarounds. Mia's team is exhausted. The pursuit of a perfect process delayed a rollout that could have been learning and improving in the field.

A: Acknowledge that the concern is real — and that you share it. Validate the uncertainty without minimizing it. Commit to working through it together and advocate upward for role clarity before the next communication goes out.
B: Be straight: some roles will change — you won't pretend otherwise. Share what's defined, what isn't, and what you're doing to influence it. Commit to a regular cadence of honest updates.

C: Briefly acknowledge the fear, then anchor in why this transformation exists — outcomes for clients, speed for the business, sustainability for the organization. Invite this group to shape how AI gets implemented, positioning them as guides, not passengers.
D: Set the agenda aside. Tell the group the strategy can wait — this can't. Listen without solving. Take notes. Commit to bringing what you hear to leadership before next steps are announced.
Moment 4: When Your Team Is Afraid of Being Replaced by AI

Indigo has announced an enterprise-wide AI transformation. Lending and underwriting, wealth management, risk and compliance — significant changes are coming. Leadership has been clear: this is the direction.

You're in what was supposed to be a strategy alignment session with your direct reports — all senior leaders themselves, each managing large teams now asking hard questions.

Before you get through the agenda, one of your most respected peers puts it plainly: "I need to ask you directly — are we being replaced? Because that's the question I can't answer for my people right now." These are experienced leaders — not panicking but watching you closely. They know the initiative is real. Some roles will shift. The full picture isn't defined. And their teams are looking to them for answers they don't have.

What do you do?
Moment 4: When Your Team Is Afraid of Being Replaced by AI
Validates the room; these leaders feel seen — increasing their capacity to show up for their own teams. But solidarity without direction can deepen the sense that no one is steering.
Trust-building through honesty. Leaders can handle the truth — and will respect you for it. But naming uncertainty without reassurance can fracture confidence in the initiative, and in you.
Purpose moves people through fear, not around it. But leading with mission before the emotional reality lands can feel like deflection — and leaders notice that.

Creates conditions for real trust. You leave knowing what this group fears — making your advocacy upward specific and credible. But the timeline doesn't pause, and leaders leaving without direction may read it as: the organization doesn't have one.
